segments.say: Starting a business takes courage. You invest time, money and often your heart into an idea, with no guarantee it will work. To do that, you probably need a healthy dose of optimism. But how optimistic are new business owners, really? And how does that compare with what usually happens?

In nineteen eighty eight, researchers Arnold Cooper, Carolyn Woo and William Dunkelberg surveyed nearly three thousand new business owners in the United States. They asked them to rate their own chances of success. And also the chances of success of businesses like theirs in general.

show.who: Arnold Cooper, Carolyn Woo & William Dunkelberg
show.where: Published in the Journal of Business Venturing, 1988
show.what: Nearly 3,000 new business owners in the United States rated their own chances of success, and the chances of a typical business like theirs.

segments.say: The results were striking. According to the study, around eighty one percent of the entrepreneurs rated their own chances of success at seven out of ten or better. And about a third rated their chances as ten out of ten. Certain success. Even though the same people rated the chances for businesses like theirs, in general, much lower.

That gap is a perfect example of what we explored in our first episode, the optimism bias, and the better than average effect. Other businesses face risks. Mine is different. The general statistics apply to others, not to me. It's a very human way of thinking. And in entrepreneurship, it may even be necessary.

show.title: New business owners rating their own odds at 10 out of 10
show.label: while seeing much lower odds for businesses like theirs

segments.say: Because without optimism, many businesses would never be started. If every founder looked only at the base rates, many would give up before they began. And some of those businesses become wonderful successes, creating jobs, products and joy. Optimism is part of the engine of progress.

But optimism can also lead people to invest more than they can afford to lose. To borrow too much. To ignore warning signs. To keep going when the numbers clearly say stop. Remember Concorde, and the trap of too much invested to quit. Founders, with their love of what they've built, can be especially vulnerable.

So perhaps the wisest approach is hope with a safety net. Be optimistic about your idea, but realistic about your finances. Limit how much you risk. Keep some savings separate. Decide in advance what would make you stop or change direction. Let your heart drive the vision, and your head guard the money.

Interestingly, research on entrepreneurs has found that many successful founders didn't succeed on their first attempt. They learned from earlier ventures that didn't work out. In that light, a business that fails isn't necessarily a waste. It can be tuition, as we said earlier. The key is to survive financially, so you can try again.

This applies beyond business owners. Anyone starting a big project, a renovation, a career change, a creative venture, faces the same mix of optimism and risk. Feeling confident is wonderful. Just make sure that if things don't go as planned, the fall won't be catastrophic.

I think the lovely balance is to be both brave and careful. Brave enough to try. Careful enough to protect yourself if it doesn't work. Many of the happiest stories of success are told by people who managed both.

So here's what research on founders teaches us. Around eighty one percent rated their own chances at seven out of ten or better. About a third felt certain of success. Optimism fuels both progress and risk. And the wisest approach may be hope with a safety net, brave enough to try, careful enough to survive.

show.title: The optimism of founders
items: 81% rated their odds at 7/10 or better

segments.say: And sometimes, the thing that steers our money decisions isn't hope or fear of loss, but fear of regret. The fear of looking back and wishing we'd chosen differently. Let's look at how regret shapes our choices, and what research says we tend to regret most.
